concepts.title: Genetic Mapping and the Centimorgan
concepts.definition: A genetic map orders loci by how often they recombine: crossover analysis of progeny phenotypes yields recombination frequencies, one percent of which defines one map unit, the centimorgan; because only well-known phenotypic loci can be tested, such maps stay coarse and call for the finer physical maps that follow.
concepts.key_idea: Recombinant offspring as a percent of the total prices the distance - each percent is one centimorgan.
question_patterns: a testcross yields 18 recombinant offspring among 200 progeny - find the recombination frequency and the map distance in centimorgan
define the map unit and state what one centimorgan represents in crossover terms
why is a genetic map described as coarsely grained or sparsely populated
how does the recombination frequency relate to the distance between two loci
what phenotype data are needed to construct a genetic map
two loci recombine at 5 percent - what does that suggest about their linkage

solution_steps.explain: Divide recombinant progeny by the total and scale to percent.
Parental offspring make up the rest of the progeny.

worked_examples.q: One percent recombination defines what map unit: the centimorgan or the metre?

concepts.title: Physical Mapping with RFLP and STS
concepts.definition: Physical maps anchor landmarks on real DNA: restriction sites whose cuts yield countable fragments (one cut in a circle gives one fragment, two cuts two; a linear molecule gives cuts plus one), length-variable microsatellite and minisatellite arrays read as SSLPs, and sequence tagged sites of 200-500 bp proven unique by PCR - Southern hybridisation taming the lakh of fragments a mammalian genome would otherwise shatter into.
concepts.key_idea: Each additional cut adds one linear fragment; circles only fragment from the first cut onward.
question_patterns: a linear DNA molecule is cut at 4 sites by BamHI - how many fragments result
how many fragments does a single cut make in a circular plasmid and in a linear chromosome
what is a sequence tagged site and why does PCR confirm its presence
how do microsatellites and minisatellites serve as SSLP map features
why must Southern hybridisation accompany RFLP analysis of large mammalian genomes
compare the resolution of genetic maps with physical maps and say why both are needed

solution_steps.explain: Every cut in a linear molecule adds one fragment to the pieces.
A circle needs its first cut just to open, then each further cut adds one fragment.

worked_examples.q: Two cuts in a circular DNA yield how many fragments?

concepts.title: First-Generation Sequencing by Capillary
concepts.definition: First-generation sequencing builds clone-by-clone: pulse-field gels split chromosomes, BAC or YAC clones carry overlapping fragments, and chain-termination chemistry reads each plasmid subclone through a capillary that reports 800-1000 fluorescent bases per run - 96 capillaries working in parallel top out near 96,000 bases per machine per run, precise but slow and costly.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply the per-capillary read by the capillary count to size one machine run, then divide the genome by it for the workload.
question_patterns: a capillary reads 1000 bases and a machine runs 96 capillaries - compute the bases sequenced per run
describe the clone-by-clone workflow from pulse field gel electrophoresis to subcloning
how does chain termination sequencing reveal each base position in the chromatogram
why did first-generation sequencing make whole genomes prohibitively expensive
which high-capacity vectors carry the overlapping fragments of the first-generation workflow
what does the colour of each chromatogram peak represent

solution_steps.explain: Parallel capillaries each deliver one read per run.
Genome bases divided by the per-run output gives runs needed.

worked_examples.q: A capillary run reports about how many bases: 800-1000 or 8?

concepts.title: Nanopore and Illumina Sequencing Reads
concepts.definition: Second-generation platforms such as Illumina amplify bridges on a flow cell and read fluorescent bases one at a time in millions of parallel reactions, but only 75-300 bases per read; third-generation nanopore sequencing instead threads a single strand through a porin pore with a helicase motor, translating each base's current disruption into sequence - real-time, field-deployable and reaching reads a megabase long.
concepts.key_idea: Divide the nanopore read length by the Illumina read length to price the long-read advantage.
question_patterns: an Illumina read covers 150 bases while a nanopore read spans 1 megabase - compute the fold difference in read length
how does bridge amplification build clusters on the Illumina flow cell
why do fluorescently tagged dNTPs reveal one base at a time in second-generation sequencing
what current change does each DNA base cause while passing through a nanopore
why is nanopore sequencing useful for field genotyping
list the advantages next-generation methods hold over chain-termination sequencing

solution_steps.explain: The quotient measures the long-read advantage.
Subtracting the short read from the long read shows the extra span covered.

worked_examples.q: Which platform threads single strands through a protein pore: nanopore or Illumina?

concepts.title: Whole Genome Targeted and Metagenomics Sequencing
concepts.definition: Sequencing projects come in flavours: whole genome sequencing - reference-guided or de novo - reads everything from Haemophilus influenzae onward including the 1990-2003 human effort; targeted and clinical exome sequencing PCR-amplify only disease-linked regions; RNASeq counts transcripts, ChipSeq maps regulator binding; and metagenomics sequences whole microbial communities straight from gut, spring or soil without culturing, hunting novel heat-stable enzymes.
concepts.key_idea: Match the project to the question - everything, a panel, the transcriptome, binding sites or a whole community.
question_patterns: differentiate reference based from de novo whole genome sequencing
why is clinical exome sequencing cheaper than whole genome sequencing for diagnostics
what does an RNASeq read count reveal about gene expression
what does a ChipSeq project map across the genome
why does metagenomics skip culturing and what challenge does it pose for data analysis
which genome was the first whole genome sequenced and when was the human sequence published
how can metagenomics of hot springs yield industrially useful enzymes

solution_steps.explain: Whole genome, targeted panel, transcriptome, binding sites or community metagenome.
Genomic DNA, PCR-amplified regions or cDNA from RNA feeds the sequencer.
Assemble or align, then count, map or bin sequences into biological insight.

worked_examples.q: Sequencing a whole microbial community straight from the gut is called what: metagenomics or genomics?

concepts.title: Genome Editing with Transposons and CRISPR-Cas9
concepts.definition: Genome engineering rewrites DNA on purpose: engineered transposons - the cut-and-paste jumping genes - knock out genes by insertional disruption or knock in new sequences, while the CRISPR-Cas9 system pairs a guide RNA with Cas9 endonuclease to cut a chosen site, letting non-homologous end joining knock the gene out or homologous recombination with a supplied template knock in the corrected version - the bacterial immune memory repurposed by Charpentier and Doudna's 2020 Nobel work.
concepts.key_idea: Position the cut with a guide RNA, then let the cell's repair choice decide knockout or precise knock-in.
question_patterns: how does transposon insertion knock out an existing gene
explain the roles of guide RNA and Cas9 endonuclease in genome editing
differentiate the repair outcomes of non-homologous end joining and homologous recombination after a double strand break
what natural bacterial function did CRISPR-Cas9 evolve from
who won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for genetic scissors and for what discovery
what is a knock-in and how does a supplied template guide the edit
why are knock-out and knock-in models valuable for drug development

solution_steps.explain: Guide RNA base-pairs the locus and recruits Cas9 to cut both strands.
Error-prone joining disrupts the gene; template-guided recombination writes the desired edit.
Knock-out or knock-in models confirm the gene's function.

worked_examples.q: Which endonuclease pairs with a guide RNA to cut DNA: Cas9 or ligase?

concepts.title: Structural Functional and Comparative Genomics
concepts.definition: Computational genomics turns sequence floods into biology on GPU-accelerated clusters, with three lenses: structural genomics solves or organises the 3D folds of every encoded protein and the physical layout of chromosomes; functional genomics asks what the genome does through RNASeq, ChipSeq and metagenomics; comparative genomics aligns species to find core and unique genes, annotate new genomes and root phylogenies - supported by India's three national genomics core facilities.
concepts.key_idea: One genome, three questions - what shape, what job, and what is shared or unique among relatives.
question_patterns: differentiate the two meanings of structural genomics held by protein and chromosome researchers
which tools and projects drive functional genomics studies of a cell state
how does comparative genomics annotate a newly sequenced genome
what are core genome genes and species-unique genes in a comparative analysis
name the three national genomics core facilities established in India and their hosts
how do BLAST ClustalW and Phylip support evolutionary comparison of genomes
what role do GPU and CUDA programming play in computational genomics

solution_steps.explain: Structure, function or comparison frames the analysis.
Homology search, annotation and multi-sequence alignment on high-performance clusters.
Folds, functions, core and unique genes, and phylogenetic lineages emerge.

worked_examples.q: Which genomics lens asks what the genome does: functional or structural?

concepts.title: Protein Engineering from Tags to Immunotoxins
concepts.definition: Rational protein engineering rewrites codons for new tricks: a Met-to-Ala point mutation at position 222 makes the detergent enzyme subtilisin bleach-proof while its Ser221-His64-Asp32 triad keeps cutting; a fused six-histidine tag grabs nickel columns for one-step purification; a GFP fusion glows to reveal where a protein lives; single-chain variable fragments fused to Pseudomonas or diphtheria toxins build immunotoxins that hunt cancer cells; and mouse antibodies are humanised for therapy.
concepts.key_idea: Change the codon, change the property - stability, purification handles, location tags or targeted cell killers.
question_patterns: why does replacing Met 222 with alanine make subtilisin stable in bleach
name the catalytic triad residues of subtilisin and their positions
how does a 6-His-tag enable purification of a recombinant protein on a nickel column
how does a GFP fusion reveal the cellular localisation of a protein
describe the construction of a recombinant immunotoxin from scFv and a toxin fragment
why must mouse monoclonal antibodies be humanised before therapeutic use in humans
what is site directed mutagenesis and how does it introduce a point mutation at a chosen codon

solution_steps.explain: Identify the amino acid whose chemistry limits or enables the desired property.
Point-mutate its codon or fuse tag, GFP, toxin or human antibody segments by rDNA methods.
Bleach-stable detergents, His-tag purification, localisation imaging or targeted cancer killing follow.

worked_examples.q: Which tag grabs nickel columns for one-step purification: six-histidine or green fluorescent?

extracted_variables.genome_bases: total bases in the target genome

solution_template.explain: All capillaries deliver their reads in the same run.
Genome size over the per-run output gives the number of runs.

worked_examples.source_ref: lebt105.txt sections 5.2.2-5.2.3 (75-300 base reads versus megabase nanopore reads)
worked_examples.question_pattern: An Illumina read covers {illumina_len} bases while a nanopore read spans {nanopore_len} bases. Find the fold length advantage of the nanopore read and the extra bases it covers in one read.

solution_template.explain: The quotient prices the long-read advantage.
The difference is the extra span one nanopore read covers.
